newsitem.title: USA: Dollar slides along with stocks, bonds.
newsitem.headline: Dollar slides along with stocks, bonds.

text.p: The dollar fell broadly Thursday along with other financial markets as currency dealers sold dollar holdings ahead of the Easter holiday weekend.
"It's a follow-through of yesterday's technical sell-off, thin holiday trade, and some long-dollar people getting out," said Russ Lascala, head of spot trading at Citibank.
"It all seems to be the same scenario -- stocks and bonds are down, the dollar is getting hit, it's Armageddon," he quipped.
The dollar fell to 1.6735 German marks in late trade Thursday from Wednesday's 1.6876 close and to 123.48 Japanese yen from 124.11.

Meanwhile, the Dow Jones industrial average had shed over 125 points by late trade. The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond fell 1-1/4 points, sending its yield up to 7.09 percent from 6.98 percent on Wednesday.
Foreign exchange trading wound down early ahead of the long Easter weekend. Normal trading will resume Monday.

A rash of upbeat U.S. economic data releases covering consumer sentiment, home sales, and help wanted advertising, strengthened the argument for another increase in interest rates by the Federal Reserve, which which weighed on bonds and, in turn, the dollar.
On Tuesday, the Fed raised rates by a quarter point -- the first increase in more than two years.
"The upbeat data shows there may be too much of a good thing so we will actually have to have (monetary) policy aimed at cooling that," said Lisa Finstrom, an analyst at Smith Barney.
"That takes away one of the plusses for the dollar," she said, referring to a strong U.S. economy.
The dollar slipped in Asian business after U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers expressed concern over Japan's trade surplus with the United States.
Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin will visit Japan on April 4 for talks in which the nagging trade tensions are expected to feature prominently.
However, renewed concerns over the health of the Japanese banking system came to the aid of the dollar.
Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi said Thursday its wholly owned U.S. subsidiary, Tokyo-Mitsubishi Derivative Products (USA), booked an appraisal loss of $50 million last year on swap trades.
Subsequently, reports that Nippon Credit Bank would soon announce a restructuring plan comforted the markets and bolstered the yen against the dollar.
The dollar also fell victim to a rebound in the German mark against other European and Asian currencies in late U.S. trade, dealers said.

Earlier, the mark had weakened against the Italian lira after Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi's cabinet approved a mini-budget in a bid to rein in the state deficit and earn Italy a place among the first wave of countries signing up to the European single currency.
In other trading, the dollar fell to 1.4480 Swiss francs from 1.4625 but rose to Canadian $1.3788 from C$1.3737. The British pound inched higher to $1.6315 from $1.6305.
